(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before we proceed with the order of the day, I wish to call your attention and that of the government to the extremely painful conditions under which the people of Laprairie are labouring just now, owing to the ice floe and damages consequent thereon, through the flood, which occurred during the night of Saturday last. In order to conform.to the rules of the House, I shall, if necessary, move the adjournment.
Every year, the village, and even the parish of Laprairie, are threatened with damages on account of more or less serious floods ; and I believe that it is with cause that for fifteen years, and under the conservative rule, the government had improvements made with a view to protecting the property and lives of the villagers. Those improvements consist in a wooden pier or rampart built along the shore so as to protect private property ; besides, ice-breakers have been constructed with a view to protecting the pier itself. Unfortunately, those structures are made of wood, and owing to the yearly floods and to age, the woodwork is altogether decayed. So, it has been decided to replace those structures by others of more durable material. At my suggestion the government have acted on the report of one of their engineers, and, last year, the minister of Public Works ordered that those wooden structures, which has become altogether inefficient should he replaced by others in concrete.
I may say at once that for a number ot years, this House has voted subsidies aggregating altogether $75,000 or $100,000, to protect the village of Laprairie. The liberal

government, on that point, followed the precedent originating with the conservative government, some fifteen years ago, and have applied the principle laid down by their predecessors.
As a matter of fact, since 1897, a considerable amount, aggregating about $50,000, lias been applied, at my request to these protection works, and last year again a large amount was voted for that purpose. Unfortunately, that amount was not voted until late last autumn, on account of the protracted session ; and there was not enough time left to carry through the necessary improvements for the protection of the village of Laprairie. As the rampart or guard pier could not be completed, a gap was left, through which the ice forced its way a few days ago, causing the damage to which I have just referred. For the time being, 'Laprairie is not to be recognized ; houses have been cut in two and carried from one side of the road to the other ; all. with the exception of five or six are submerged as high up as the second story ; clothing, furniture have suffered from water. If no deaths have occurred, some narrow escapes are recorded. Women had to flee in the darkness of night, carrying away their children in spite of many difficulties, and one of them having let lier infant slip into the water, it was only through a miracle that it was rescued and restored to life.
I suppose there is no necessity for me to appeal to anything else but the government's equal force to their sense' of justice. If the breaking of the ice had such terrible results at Laprairie, this year, it is due, as I have just stated, first to the ineffectiveness of the guard pier,-in respect of which no fault can be found with the government, but also to the building up of that million dollar island, in other words that long dike which starts at Victoria bridge and extends into tile river. That dike or pier was built by order of the harbour commissioners, and by narrowing the bed of the St. Lawrence has always gi ven rise to inundations of a more disastrous character than formerly.
When its construction was begun, protests came from Laprairie, St. Lambert and a great many citizens on the south shore. It was urged that the construction of that dike should not be proceeded with, as disasters were apprehended; and what was the result? In winter time, there, water does not freeze any longer for a month or a month and a half; so we have no more that ice bridge over which farmers used formerly to cross when taking their products to Montreal. The water no Jonger freezes, and instead of driving in direct line towards Bonsecours market, as formerly, they cross to Point St. Charles and have to reach the market through the streets of Montreal, thus undergoing all the inconveniences which arise from circulating along thoroughfares cut up by double tracks of electric railways.

It would be an easy matter to my mind, to start in a craft of that kind from Quebec-where winter navigation is a fact-about the first of March and to 'ascend the St. Lawrence, breaking the ice as high up as Montreal, and keeping an open channel for the ice and water to flow down freely. I believe that, by that means, the river would keep its level and floods would be avoided. Another advantage would result from that : the opening of navigation would be hastened by two or three weeks, and might without difficulty, take place about the first of April, for the benefit not only of the port of Montreal, but of the whole country. For instance, if it were a recognized fact that by the first of April every year, the port of Montreal or the St. -"Lawrence route were open, that would be a distinct gain for us.
As far as the Department of Marine is concerned, I may say right here that I am collecting the necessary data to enable me to lay before the House a report from which we may ascertain whether the present state of things could not be remedied.
I think that is the most practical way to reach good results.

In rising, Mr. Speaker, to speak on tills question, I do not think it necessary, as most of the members of the opposition seem to do, to review every detail of the contract which was adopted last year. I only' intend making a few remarks, as a representative from the province of Quebec, to answer the call advanced by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). As has been said already, there is no use for our friends who sit on your left, Mr. Speaker, trying to conceal their disappointment over the amendments made to the Transcontinental Act this session. They seemed to expect that the concessions made would be so intolerable to the country as to render the construction of the railway impossible. Finding that this is not the case, finding that the amendments do not change the nature of the contract but merely some of its accidents, they have resorted to the tactics of emptying all the vials of their wrath on the eastern section. They seem to think, most of them with great joy, that in these new amendments lies the capital condemnation of that part of the railway which the government is to construct. Well, Mr. Speaker, I cannot say that I share that view. On the contrary I am of the opinion that these amendments will assure in the near future the construction of that part of the railway. I will surprise, no doubt, many on the other side in stating that I am a believer in the theory that the eastern division of the road is as necessary to the country as the western part of it, and, Sir, I have strengthened that conviction from speeches I have heard on the other side of the House. Mr. Speaker, in a day or two every member of this House will be called upon to vote on the resolution brought forward by the right hon. the Prime Minister and the amendment to it proposed by the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). This is a time in the history of Canada when one has to ask himself what are the duties and responsibilities devolving upon a member of this House upon political questions involving the welfare of the whole Dominion. During the past six or seven years there has been a growing disposition, at least in the part of the country I have the honour to represent, to wonder how far this government, in dealing with matters of national importance, will go in ignoring all business rules and all the reasons that would guide parties in business transactions in private life. If we wanted to select an example of the extent to which the government would dare to go in violating and disregarding all business rules, we have it in the proposition put forward by the government last year and the still worse proposition now before us in regard to the so-called transcontinental railway scheme. We find that members of parliament are called upon to vote for an expenditure which has been estimated by several gentlemen sitting on your left, Mr. Speaker, to amount to nine-tenths of the total cost of the largest work ever undertaken by the Dominion of Canada. And it has been demonstrated that the other party in this enterprise, who is called upon to pay only one-tenth of the cost, is to have the whole benefit for fifty years, while the other partner, who puts in nine-tenths of the cost, is to have no benefit whatever for fifty years. At the end of that time, if they are*, alive, or if their descendants are not all in the asylum for having voted for such a scheme, they will be allowed to make an arrangement for dividing up what is left.
This scheme was debated fully at the last session of this House, and I do not propose to weary the House by going into the details of it. But I have a little hope that if I say a few words on the question, some of the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House may begin to feel that they will not be doing their duty to the country, or to those parts of the country which they represent ffthey do not insist on the government withdrawing the scheme, and getting a mandate from Z people before they plungei the country into an enormous expenditure for which the country gets practically nothing in retu .

not a word about tbe Intercolonial being given any. protection either now or then. It is to go along, I suppose, by virtue of the special taxes to be contributed by the loyal people of Canada in order to keep it going.
Now, Sir, the question has been asked to-night by the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Clancy), where is the Minister of Railways and Canals ? Well, I do not wish to emphasize any more than my hon. friend has done the significance of the absence of that hon. minister, but I. as a humble member of this House, feel that the Minister of Railways and Canals ought not to have signed this contract if he was not going to come into the House and explain to us why he signed it. I feel that the Minister of Railways and Canals is not doing justice to himself if he is not prepared to come in here and explain and defend this contract, and to listen to the arguments that are used pro and con in regard to this railway. Does the Minister of Railways and Canals know all about it ? Has he considered carefully what the effect of it is ? He went down to St. John not long ago and received a strong hint that the people did not want it. He went down there and did his best to bring a supporter back here on the strength of this scheme, and he came back empty, but the leader of the opposition got a supporter instead of the Minister of Railways and Canals. I should think the Minister of Railways and Canals would begin to learn something from his intercourse with the people in regard to this matter. If he kept in closer touch with the people he might come to the conclusion that they are not in favour of this scheme. Perhaps the minister has not yet made up his mind to do like his predecessor and resign but he is waiting to see whether the government will not undertake to withdraw this contract. Perhaps they will, perhaps they will not. Rut I think the Minister of Railways and Canals ought not to remain out of the House as he does day after day, and night after night during this discussion, because the people will take the meaning to be that he is not in favour of this scheme, and I am satisfied that they will be nearer right than wrong, particularly after they read what he said last session, as it has been quoted by my hon. friend from Bothwell.
Now the government supporters do make an attempt to say that this scheme ought to go through. I want to be quite fair with them. I am willing to concede them everything they can get out of this argument. And they do make an attempt to show that this road should go through. Their chief argument is that the road is needed. Now I may say that there is no dispute between us on that point. We do not say that a road of some kind is not needed, but these gentlemen seem to think that as long as they say to the people, you need a road, then we are justified in paying nine-tenths

But we ought not to be troubled about Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories or British Columbia in this parliament. We are working for the people of Canada from Halifax to Vancouver. This is the way the hon. leader of the opposition deals with the fiscal question, as with every other question ; he says the same thing in one part of the country as he does in another. I want to tell the Solicitor General that there is a Conservative party in Canada, and there always will be. From what I can see, there is a very large and active Conservative party in the province of Quebec, and 1 have no doubt that he will find it more active than he wants it to be as soon as the government give the people a chance to say what they think of this matter.
Now, I have just one word more to say. I am going to do what I have done before, hopelessly perhaps, but still I think it my duty to keep on doing it. I am going to appeal to this government, humble member as I am-for I know a little about the feeling of my own constituency, and I have no doubt that it is the same in the rest of this Dominion-I am going to appeal to them to do something in the interest of Canada, and not to be troubled about party exigencies. I am going to ask them if they do not think that the cost of this scheme of theirs to the people of Canada will not have the eftect of dismissing them from office. I am going ask them not to put upon the people ot Canada the necessity of being defendants in a suit for breach of contract in the Exchequei Court The Grand Trunk Pacific Company said io them : We are not satisfied with the contract which was made last yeai ,

now give us a better one ; true, it is against the interests of the people of Canada ; but give it before you go to the country, because if you do not, you cannot give it afterwards. I appeal to this government not to put the people of Canada in the position of being defendants in an action for breach of contract, because I tell them that if they pass this measure, then after the next election when the leader of the opposition comes back and forms a cabinet, the first thing he will do will be to repudiate that contract, because the people will have put him in power to do so; and as soon as that is done, we may have to pay $50,000 or $100,000 of damages to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company for breaking that contract. I am quite sure that the people of this country would much rather have to pay out of the exchequer the damages which the Grand Trunk Pacific Company could prove they had sustained by making surveys and by the disappointment they had suffered, than the greater evil of this bad bargain which the government are attempting to put upon them. Because as soon as the people get the chance to show what their mandate is, there is no doubt that their mandate will be to cancel the contract, even if they have to pay $50,000 or $100,000 to do it rather than $150,000,000 in return for which they get nothing. I do not think it is necessary or wise that I should detain the House any longer. I have said in a hurried way what I have had to say on this matter. I think we have calmly to consider this question as a business proposition; not voting for it because the Grand Trunk Company want it or because the premier happens to have asked us to do so-because the premier of this country may make mistakes, and the people are not going to let their representatives support him in those mistakes. The people of the Dominion of Canada expect the premier, no matter whether he be Liberal or Conserative in politics, to serve the interests of the people and to see that the assets and property of this Dominion are not wasted, as this resolution would waste them.
